hints.content:
We can map a figure onto a **similar** figure using only rigid transformations and dilations. This means the figures must have exactly the same shapes, but may have different sizes.

For triangles in particular, two triangles are similar if all of their corresponding angles are [[☃ definition 1]].

options.definition: Angles with the same measure that we can map onto each other using rigid transformations

hints.content:
Triangle $ABC$ has angle measures of $68^\circ$ and $58^\circ$. The third angle measure is therefore $180^\circ - 68^\circ - 58^\circ = 54^\circ$.



[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: Triangle A B C. Angle A is fifty-eight degrees. Angle B is sixty-eight degrees. Angle C is fifty-four degrees.

hints.content:
Triangle $QRS$ has angle measures of $93^\circ$ and $54^\circ$. The third angle measure is $180 ^\circ- 93^\circ - 54^\circ = 33^\circ$. 



[[☃ image 1]]

Therefore $\triangle QRS$ is not similar to $\triangle ABC$.

options.alt: Triangle Q R S. Angle Q is fifty-four degrees. Angle R is thirty-three degrees. Angle S is ninety-three degrees.

hints.content:
Triangle $TUV$ has angle measures of $58^\circ$ and $54^\circ$. The third angle measure is $180^\circ - 58^\circ - 54^\circ = 68^\circ$.



[[☃ image 1]]

Therefore $\triangle TUV$ is similar to $\triangle ABC$.

options.alt: Triangle T U V. Angle T is fifty-eight degrees. Angle U is sixty-eight degrees. Angle V is fifty-four degrees.

hints.content: In conclusion, only $\triangle TUV$ is similar to triangle $\triangle ABC$.
